Stage 3 · Language

Saying the difficult thing

Four moves that get the problem fixed without costing you the relationship.

Read these four lines from real complaints.
  • I’m sorry to have to say this, but I need to talk to you about something.
  • Look, it’s a bit awkward, but I’m afraid there’s something I’m not happy about.
  • It would really help if you could just clear up your stuff.
  • Would you mind taking the calls in your own time?
What do the first two have in common that the last two do not?
A complaint has two goals that pull against each other: fix the problem, and keep the relationship.

Complaining is one of the highest-risk things you can do in a foreign language. Say too little and nothing changes; say it too directly and you damage a working relationship. English resolves this with a fixed structure that separates the person from the behaviour and turns the request into a question.

Compare You’re always on the phone with Would you mind taking personal calls in your own time? The first attacks a character trait and leaves the other person nothing to do but defend themselves. The second names one behaviour, asks rather than tells, and leaves them a way to agree without losing face. The information is the same; the outcome usually is not.

A working complaint has four moves, and learners most often skip the first. Prepare the listener that something uncomfortable is coming (I’m sorry to have to say this, but…). Name the problem, not the person. Request a change as a question. Leave a way out (I know it might not seem such a big deal…). On the receiving end, the expected response is equally fixed: apologise, then commit to a change.

The same logic governs online discussion, which is why the two strands sit in one lesson. Disagreement in an English-language thread is normally two-part: acknowledge what the other person said, then object. I see your point, but… and That’s a fair point — however… read as reasonable; a bare contradiction reads as hostile, however correct it may be.

Before you look at the table: the table below sets out the four moves in order with the phrases that fill each one. Notice which structures take -ing — Would you mind is the one to watch.
The four moves of a complaint
The moveWhat you sayWhy
Warn themI’m sorry to have to say this, but… · Look, it’s a bit awkward, but… · Sorry to bother you, but…Nobody likes being ambushed. One second of warning changes the whole reception.
Name the problemI’ve got a problem with… · There’s something I’m not happy about.Say the thing, once, without a list of previous crimes.
Ask for the changeIt would really help if you could… · Would you mind…ing? · Do you think you could…?A complaint with no request leaves the other person guessing.
Leave a way outI know it might not seem such a big deal… · I’m sure you didn’t realize…Lets them fix it without admitting they are a bad person.
The same four moves in an online discussion
The moveIn writing
Concede firstI see your point, but… · That’s a fair point, although…
DisagreeI’d have to disagree with… · In my view,…
Give evidenceThe path has been closed off since April. · That’s four months of the year.
Ask for somethingI’d suggest… · Do you think it’s worth…ing?

Complain about the behaviour, not the person. It would really help if you could clear up your stuff is a request. You’re so untidy is a description of somebody’s character, and nobody has ever changed because of one.

Avoid always and never. You always leave your cups out invites the reply No I don’t — I washed one on Tuesday, and now you are arguing about Tuesday instead of the cups.

Would you mind takes -ing. Would you mind taking the calls outside? Not Would you mind to take. And the polite answer to it is No, of course not — which means yes.

Online, concede before you disagree. Starting with I see your point costs you nothing and buys you a reader. Starting with You’re wrong costs you the reader before your evidence arrives.

Full grammar reference — making a complaint, and taking part in an online discussion

What it is

Two related sets of functional language. The first covers complaining effectively: preparing the listener, stating the problem without accusing, requesting a change, and responding when you are on the receiving end. The second covers online discussion: entering a thread, agreeing partially, disagreeing without hostility, and closing a point.

What it means, and what it does

A complaint has two goals that pull against each other: fix the problem, and keep the relationship. English solves this by separating the person from the behaviour and by wrapping the request in a question. You’re always on the phone attacks; Would you mind taking personal calls in your own time? asks for a change and leaves the other person their dignity. The same logic governs disagreement online.

When and why we use it

Complaining is one of the highest-risk things you can do in a foreign language. Say too little and nothing changes; say it too directly and you damage a working relationship. English resolves this with a fixed structure that separates the person from the behaviour and turns the request into a question.

Compare You’re always on the phone with Would you mind taking personal calls in your own time? The first attacks a character trait and leaves the other person nothing to do but defend themselves. The second names one behaviour, asks rather than tells, and leaves them a way to agree without losing face. The information is the same; the outcome usually is not.

A working complaint has four moves, and learners most often skip the first. Prepare the listener that something uncomfortable is coming (I’m sorry to have to say this, but…). Name the problem, not the person. Request a change as a question. Leave a way out (I know it might not seem such a big deal…). On the receiving end, the expected response is equally fixed: apologise, then commit to a change.

The same logic governs online discussion, which is why the two strands sit in one lesson. Disagreement in an English-language thread is normally two-part: acknowledge what the other person said, then object. I see your point, but… and That’s a fair point — however… read as reasonable; a bare contradiction reads as hostile, however correct it may be.

Typical situations

You need this for problems with colleagues, flatmates and neighbours, for faulty goods and poor service, and for taking part in any comment thread or discussion where you do not agree with the previous speaker.

  • Preparing the listener — a warning phrase that softens what follows.I’m sorry to have to say this, but I need to talk to you about something.
  • Naming the problem — the situation, not the person’s character.I’ve got a problem with the noise in the mornings.
  • Admitting it is awkward — acknowledging the social cost.Look, it’s a bit awkward, but I’m afraid there’s something I’m not happy about.
  • Requesting a change — a question, so it can be accepted rather than obeyed.Would you mind taking the calls at lunchtime?
  • Suggesting the solution — it would really help if…It would really help if you could clear up your things.
  • Responding to a complaint — apologise, then commit.I’m sorry about that. I’ll make sure I do that next time.
  • Agreeing partially online — concede first, then qualify.That’s a fair point, but it doesn’t apply to everyone.
  • Disagreeing politely online — soften and give a reason.I see your point, but the figures say something different. I’d have to disagree.

How it differs from similar structures

Would you mind + -ing? (very polite, asks permission to ask) · Do you think you could + base verb? (polite, direct request) · Could you + base verb? (neutral). All three are usable; only the first takes -ing.
I disagree. (blunt) · I’d have to disagree. (softened by would) · I see your point, but… (softened and constructive). At B1, prefer the last two.

How to build it

Prepare: I’m sorry to have to say this, but + clause
State: I’ve got a problem with + noun / verb-ing
Request: Would you mind + verb-ing?  ·  Do you think you could + base verb?
Concede then object: I see your point, but + clause  ·  That’s a fair point, however, + clause
PreparingI’m sorry to have to say this, but… · Look, it’s a bit awkward, but…
Stating the problemI’ve got a problem with… · I’m afraid there’s something I’m not happy about.
Requesting — -ing formWould you mind taking the calls outside?
Requesting — base formDo you think you could take the calls outside?
Softening the impactI know it might not seem such a big deal, but…
Apologising in responseI’m sorry about that. I just didn’t think.
CommittingI’ll make sure I do that in future.
Online — enteringIn my view,… · From what I’ve read,…
Online — concedingThat’s a fair point. · I see what you mean.
Online — disagreeingI’d have to disagree. · I’m not so sure about that.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Would you mind is followed by -ing, and the answer is counter-intuitive: No, not at all means yes, I will. Yes, I do mind is a refusal. Learners frequently answer the wrong way round.
  • Complain about the behaviour, not the person. The kitchen gets left in a mess is easier to accept than You’re messy — and the passive is one way English achieves that distance.
  • I’m afraid here has nothing to do with fear. It is a softener that signals bad news is coming.
  • In an online post, quote or reference what you are replying to before you disagree; otherwise your reply reads as an unconnected assertion.
  • Register online is neutral, not formal: contractions are normal, but insults and all-capitals are not. The lesson’s phrases work in both a comment thread and a meeting.
  • Sorry to bother you, but… is the standard opener when you complain to a stranger, for example in a shop; I’m sorry to have to say this is for someone you know.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Would you mind to take the calls outside? → Would you mind taking the calls outside?Mind is followed by -ing.
  • — Would you mind waiting? — Yes, of course! → — Would you mind waiting? — No, not at all.No means ‘I don’t mind’ — that is the agreement.
  • You are very annoying with your phone. → I’m sorry to have to say this, but the calls are a bit disruptive.Complain about the behaviour, not the person.
  • It would really help if you can clear up. → It would really help if you could clear up.It would help if takes could, matching the conditional.
  • I’m sorry for be so annoying. → I’m sorry for being so annoying.Sorry for takes -ing.
  • I’m not agree with this post. → I don’t agree with this post.Agree is a verb and takes no be.

More examples in context

  • preparingI’m sorry to have to say this, but I need to talk to you about the phone calls.
  • awkwardnessLook, it’s a bit awkward, but I’m afraid there’s something I’m not happy about.
  • statingI’ve got a problem with this tablet — it keeps turning itself off.
  • softeningI know it might not seem such a big deal, but it does add up.
  • requestingWould you mind taking personal calls in your own time?
  • requestingDo you think you could wash your mugs before you leave?
  • suggestingIt would really help if you could just put things away in the fridge.
  • respondingI’m sorry about that — I just didn’t think. I’ll make sure I do it every time.
  • online, concedingThat’s a fair point, and I hadn’t thought about the cost.
  • online, disagreeingI see your point, but I’d have to disagree — the survey covered only 2,000 people.

A tip for remembering it

Build every complaint in four moves and never skip the first: 1 prepare (I’m sorry to have to say this, but…), 2 name the behaviour, not the person, 3 ask, don’t tell (Would you mind…?), 4 leave a way out (I know it might not seem a big deal…). Online, add one move at the start: show you have read what you are replying to.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Prepare the listener before you complain: I’m sorry to have to say this, but…
  2. Name the behaviour or the situation, not the person’s character.
  3. Make the request a question: Would you mind + -ing? or Do you think you could + base verb?
  4. No, not at all is the agreement to Would you mind…?
  5. Respond to a complaint with an apology and a commitment.
  6. Online, concede before you object: I see your point, but…

Stage 5 · Main input

Disagreeing in public

Read it as a writer. You are going to post one like it.

Before you read: what makes an online disagreement worth reading?

Choose one. The model does three of these.

Re: Closing the east path — has anybody actually asked us?

@Marat I see your point about the nesting season, and that’s a fair point about the noise. But I’d have to disagree with the conclusion.

The east path has been closed off since April, and the sign they put up says it reopens in July. That is four months of the year on the only route where you can actually make out the far side of the lake. I devote most Saturdays to bird-watching there, and so do about thirty other people in this group.

There must be a reason they chose the east path rather than the north, but nobody has said what it is. The eastern hides are considerably further from the nests than the northern ones, which stay open all year.

In my view the problem isn’t the closure — it’s that nobody asked. The reserve came up with the plan in March and announced it in April.

I’d suggest two things. First, put our counts into a shared database, so that next year the decision has numbers behind it. Second, ask before closing, not after. If it happens again next April, I think it is worth making a proper campaign of it.

@Ainur — you raised this last year and nothing changed. Do you think it is worth trying again?

What the model does, in five moves
  • Agrees with two things before disagreeing with one. That is why anybody keeps reading.
  • Puts dates and numbers in — April, July, four months, thirty people.
  • Makes a deduction rather than an accusation. There must be a reason, but nobody has said what it is.
  • Names the real problem, which turns out not to be the one under discussion.
  • Asks for two specific things, and pulls another person into the conversation.

First say you had no idea. Then say that other people do it too. Then offer something smaller than what was asked for. Only agree fully if they ask a second time politely.

4 · Now write the discussion post. 150–200 words.
Your plan
  • Line 1 — agree with something the other person said. Genuinely.
  • Line 2 — say where you disagree, once.
  • Paragraph 2 — the evidence. At least two numbers or dates.
  • Paragraph 3 — what you think the real problem is.
  • Close — two specific suggestions, and a question to somebody else.
